To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there are two perspectives that frame how to account analytically for clustering in health studies, and (2) each perspective has different implications for the choice of cluster definitions to use in the analytic stage of a study.

(1) the decision of whether to account for clustering in analysis should be made based on the research question and the goals of the study (model-based versus design-based); (2) the decision of which clusters to account for should be made based upon the study design, data collection procedures, and the goals of study (model-based); and (3) the decision of how to account for clustering should be made based primarily upon the goals of the research (design-based).

(1) the model-based and design-based perspectives have distinct goals and implications for the analysis of clustered data; (2) there are tensions within each of these perspectives; (3) there are tensions between these perspectives; (4) the decision about which cluster definition to use has implications for all subsequent analytic decisions; and (5) the model-based perspective is more likely to use multiple cluster definitions and the design-based perspective is more focused on one cluster definition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to account for the clustering of health in overlapping contexts.
the implications of using different clustering definitions, particularly for model-based inference goals.
how to account for the non-independence of observations when more than one context type is indexed.

there are no conclusive statements.
the answer to the question, “Should I account for clustering?” is, “It depends,” and we provide some guidance to help researchers make that decision.
there is no conclusive statement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the choice of cluster definition is an analytic decision that is best informed by substantive theory and research questions.
there are many ways to account for clustering, and the best choice depends on the research question and the data available.
the choice of cluster definition is a crucial one, and it is one that is best made by considering the goals of inference and the nature of the data and their context.
The main takeaway from our work is that
researchers need to be aware of their analytic goals and the implications of their choices, and that the choice of cluster definition should be made with those goals in mind.

researchers should be clear about which perspective they are following, and that this perspective will guide their choice of analytic methods, their interpretation of results, and their conclusions about the health implications of their findings.
there are no “right” or “wrong” answers for the choice of clusters to account for in analysis.
